question: What first got you interested in horses, and how did that turn into wanting to study Equine Science?
lookingFor: A genuine origin story that has clearly matured from an emotional attachment into an academic interest.

bullets: Give a specific, real starting point rather than a vague 'always loved horses'
Show the shift from enjoying horses to wanting to understand them scientifically
Connect it to something concrete you have done since
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started mucking out at a local livery yard when I was twelve just to be near the horses, and I got hooked on the small daily puzzles, like why one gelding always paced before feeding time. That curiosity eventually pulled me toward the science side, so I started reading about equine behaviour and nutrition properly instead of just picking things up from the yard. Doing my work experience with an equine vet confirmed it, I wanted to understand the why behind what I was already seeing every day.

commonMistakes: Saying only 'I've loved horses since I was little' with no development
Describing pure hobby interest with no academic angle
Failing to mention any concrete experience
followUps: What is the most interesting thing you have learned about horses since that started?

question: Why do you want to study Equine Science here specifically, rather than at another university?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this course's facilities, staff, or structure, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific facility, yard, module, or member of staff
Explain why that specific thing matters to your own goals
Show you compared it against alternatives rather than applying blind
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your yard runs a teaching herd that students help manage day to day rather than just observe, and that hands-on responsibility is what I want, not another course where the practical work is optional extra credit. I also looked closely at the exercise physiology module, since I am interested in how conditioning programmes are actually built for performance horses. I compared it with two other courses and this one had the strongest balance of proper science teaching alongside real yard time, which is exactly what I am after.

commonMistakes: Praise that could apply to any equine course
Citing only location or campus appearance
No evidence of comparing against other universities
followUps: What would you want to get out of the teaching yard specifically?

question: Tell us about your hands-on experience with horses so far.
lookingFor: Concrete, varied experience with evidence of responsibility and learning, not just riding lessons.

bullets: Describe specific duties, not just 'I've ridden for years'
Show progression in responsibility over time
Reflect on one thing that experience actually taught you
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I have worked two mornings a week at a livery yard for three years, starting with mucking out and turnout and eventually being trusted to help the yard manager with feed planning for a mixed group of twelve horses. I also did two weeks of work experience with an equine physiotherapist, which let me see rehabilitation work up close. That placement taught me how much of recovery is about patient, incremental change rather than one dramatic fix, which changed how I think about horse care generally.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning riding lessons with no yard responsibility
A list of tasks with no reflection
Exaggerating responsibilities that were not really theirs
followUps: What was the hardest part of that responsibility?

question: What have you read or followed recently about the equine industry, beyond your school syllabus?
lookingFor: Evidence of independent engagement with the field and an ability to summarise and react to it critically.

bullets: Name a specific book, journal, article, or ongoing debate
Summarise the core idea or finding accurately
Give a personal reaction or opinion, not just a summary
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I have been following the debate around the whip rules in British racing after the BHA's recent reviews, and I read a few of the position papers from welfare groups alongside the racing authorities' own reports. What struck me is how much the argument comes down to differing definitions of what counts as necessary versus punitive use. I also read Sharon May-Davis's work on equine anatomy and posture, which changed how I think about saddle fit as a welfare issue rather than just a performance one.

commonMistakes: Vague reference to 'articles online' with no specifics
Summary with no personal opinion attached
Confusing equine welfare topics with general animal welfare with no equine specifics
followUps: Where do you personally land on that debate, and why?

question: Can you explain why horses are described as hindgut fermenters, and why that matters for how we feed them?
lookingFor: A correct grasp of equine digestive anatomy and its practical link to feeding management.

bullets: Explain that fibre is fermented by microbes in the caecum and colon rather than a multi-chambered stomach
Contrast briefly with ruminants like cattle
Link this to why horses need frequent forage rather than large infrequent meals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Horses have a relatively small, single-chambered stomach, so most of their fibre digestion happens later, in the caecum and large colon, where microbes ferment plant material the horse cannot break down enzymatically itself. That is different from a cow, which ferments fibre earlier in a multi-chambered stomach before the food even reaches the true stomach. Because the horse's stomach is small and produces acid continuously, it is designed for near constant trickle feeding of forage, which is why big infrequent meals or long gaps without hay increase the risk of problems like gastric ulcers and colic.

commonMistakes: Confusing horses with ruminants and describing multiple stomach chambers
Naming the caecum without explaining what actually happens there
Missing the practical feeding implication entirely
followUps: What kind of dietary change could this anatomy make risky if done too quickly?

question: Why is colic considered such a serious and common problem in horses, and what are some of its causes?
lookingFor: Understanding that colic is a symptom rather than one disease, plus awareness of common risk factors.

bullets: Explain colic is a broad term for abdominal pain, not a single diagnosis
Give at least two or three plausible causes such as impaction, gas, or spasmodic colic
Mention why the horse's gut anatomy makes it particularly prone to this
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Colic just means abdominal pain, and it can come from anything from a simple gas buildup to a serious twist in the intestine, which is why vets take every case seriously until proven mild. Common causes include sudden diet changes, poor quality or insufficient forage, dehydration, and sand ingestion in some regions, all of which disrupt the delicate gut microbiome. Horses are especially prone to it partly because of their long, mobile intestines and limited ability to vomit, so a blockage or gas buildup has few ways to resolve itself naturally.

commonMistakes: Treating colic as one specific disease rather than a symptom
Naming only one cause
Not connecting it back to any anatomical reason horses are vulnerable
followUps: What signs might indicate a colic case is a surgical emergency?

question: If you were asked to assess whether a horse was lame, what would you actually look for?
lookingFor: A structured, observational approach showing familiarity with basic gait assessment, not vague guessing.

bullets: Mention watching the horse in walk and trot, ideally on a hard, straight surface
Reference head-nodding for forelimb lameness and hip-hike or drop for hindlimb
Note the value of comparing both directions and consulting a vet or farrier for confirmation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would want to watch the horse trot in a straight line on a firm, level surface, because lameness often shows up more clearly at trot than walk. For a front-leg lameness you typically see the head nod down as the sound leg lands, since the horse is trying to take weight off the sore limb, while hindlimb lameness often shows as an uneven hip movement instead. I would also want to see the horse on both reins and possibly lunged, since some lamenesses only appear on a circle, but I would always want a vet or experienced farrier to confirm rather than relying on my eye alone.

commonMistakes: Only describing limping with no detail on which limb or gait to check
Ignoring the difference between forelimb and hindlimb signs
Overstating confidence in diagnosing without professional input
followUps: Why might lameness be harder to spot on a soft surface than a hard one?

question: What can you tell us about the mare's oestrous cycle and roughly how long a pregnancy lasts in horses?
lookingFor: Basic factual command of equine reproductive physiology.

bullets: State that mares are seasonally polyoestrous, cycling mainly in spring and summer
Give an approximate cycle length, around 21 days, with oestrus lasting several days
Give gestation length, roughly eleven months or about 340 days
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Mares are seasonally polyoestrous, meaning they cycle repeatedly but mainly during the longer daylight months of spring and summer, which is driven by changing light exposure affecting their hormones. A typical cycle is around twenty-one days, with the mare in season, or oestrus, for roughly five to seven days of that. Gestation is unusually long for a domestic animal, at about eleven months, so breeders have to plan foaling dates carefully around when they want the foal born the following spring.

commonMistakes: Confusing gestation length with the cycle length
Not mentioning the seasonal aspect at all
Giving wildly inaccurate numbers with no ballpark accuracy
followUps: Why do breeders often want foals born as early in the year as possible?

question: Can you explain, in simple terms, how coat colour is inherited in horses? A basic example is fine.
lookingFor: Basic grasp that coat colour follows genetic inheritance patterns, using a correct simple example.

bullets: Explain that a base coat gene, such as black or red, is modified by other genes
Give one concrete correct example, like the extension gene or the grey gene
Acknowledge some patterns are more genetically complex than a single gene
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Coat colour in horses starts from a base coat, which is essentially black or chestnut depending on which version of the extension gene the horse carries, and then other genes modify that base. The grey gene is a good simple example, it is dominant, so a horse with even one copy will progressively grey out with age regardless of its original colour underneath. Some patterns like dilution genes or spotting are more complex and can involve multiple genes interacting, so I know coat colour genetics is not always as simple as a single dominant or recessive trait.

commonMistakes: Describing colour inheritance as random rather than gene-based
Confusing greying with white spotting patterns
Overclaiming certainty about a complex trait that is actually polygenic
followUps: Why might a grey foal be born a completely different colour at birth?

question: Horses are often described as flight animals. What does that mean in practice for how we handle and train them?
lookingFor: Understanding of horses as prey animals and how that shapes safe, low-stress handling practice.

bullets: Explain the evolutionary basis, horses are prey animals with flight as their main defence
Give a practical handling implication, like approaching calmly and avoiding sudden movements
Connect it to training approaches that work with, not against, that instinct
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: As a prey species, a horse's default response to something startling is to run first and figure out the danger later, which is very different from a predator species that might stop and investigate. In practice that means handlers need to move predictably, give the horse time to see and process new objects, and avoid cornering them, since a frightened horse without an escape route can panic badly. Good training methods, like desensitisation and pressure and release, work precisely because they let the horse learn that standing still and staying calm is safe, rather than fighting that flight instinct.

commonMistakes: Describing horses as simply 'nervous' with no biological reasoning
Giving no practical handling implication
Suggesting flight response can just be trained away entirely rather than managed
followUps: How might herd dynamics affect how a horse reacts when handled alone versus in a group?

question: Why is it significant that horses are obligate nasal breathers?
lookingFor: Correct anatomical fact plus understanding of its consequences for exercise and health.

bullets: State that horses cannot breathe through their mouth, unlike humans
Explain the consequence for airway problems during exercise, like nasal restriction or laryngeal issues
Link this to why respiratory disease can seriously limit athletic performance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Horses cannot breathe through their mouths at all, their soft palate seals off that route, so all of their air has to move through the nasal passages even at maximum exertion. That makes any restriction, whether it is a physical narrowing, inflammation, or a condition like laryngeal hemiplegia, a much bigger problem for a horse than it would be for us, because there is no backup airway to compensate. It is part of why respiratory soundness is checked so carefully in performance horses, since even a small airway restriction can significantly limit how much oxygen they can take in during fast work.

commonMistakes: Assuming horses can breathe through their mouth like humans can
Stating the fact without explaining why it matters
Confusing respiratory anatomy with digestive anatomy
followUps: Can you name a condition that affects the equine airway during exercise?

question: What is laminitis, and why is it such a serious welfare concern?
lookingFor: Correct basic understanding of laminitis and its impact on the horse, with awareness of risk factors.

bullets: Explain laminitis as inflammation of the laminae connecting the hoof wall to the pedal bone
Note it can lead to pain, rotation, or sinking of the pedal bone in severe cases
Mention at least one common trigger, such as excess sugar intake or obesity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Laminitis is inflammation of the laminae, the tissue that bonds the hoof wall to the pedal bone inside the foot, and when that bond weakens the pedal bone can rotate or even sink within the hoof capsule. It is extremely painful because the horse's full weight is bearing down on inflamed, sensitive tissue with nowhere to go, and severe cases can become career-ending or even life-threatening. It is often triggered by things like sudden access to lush spring grass, obesity, or conditions like equine metabolic syndrome, which is why diet management is such a central part of prevention.

commonMistakes: Confusing laminitis with general lameness or a hoof abscess
Not explaining the pedal bone connection at all
Omitting any mention of dietary or metabolic risk factors
followUps: What management changes would you suggest for a pony at high risk of laminitis?

question: How would you approach building a fitness programme for a horse returning to work after an injury?
lookingFor: Awareness of gradual, structured conditioning principles and the physiology behind them.

bullets: Mention starting with controlled walking and building duration before intensity
Reference the different recovery rates of tissues, such as tendons taking longer than muscle
Show awareness that monitoring, like vet checkups or heart rate, should guide progression
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would start very conservatively with controlled walking exercise, usually in hand or on a horse walker, and only build up duration before ever adding speed or trot work. That is because soft tissues like tendons and ligaments heal much more slowly and with lower blood supply than muscle, so pushing intensity too soon is one of the most common causes of reinjury. I would want the programme built alongside a vet, using regular checks and things like heart rate recovery to guide when it is genuinely safe to progress, rather than following a fixed calendar regardless of how the horse is actually responding.

commonMistakes: Suggesting a fixed timeline with no reference to tissue healing differences
Jumping straight to fast work without a walking foundation
Ignoring the need for veterinary input during rehabilitation
followUps: Why do tendon injuries in particular carry a high risk of recurrence?

question: What is body condition scoring, and why is it a useful tool in managing horses?
lookingFor: Basic understanding of a practical welfare and nutrition assessment tool used in the industry.

bullets: Explain it as a hands-on visual and palpation method for assessing fat cover
Mention key areas checked, like the ribs, neck, and rump
Link it to preventing both obesity and underweight-related problems
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Body condition scoring is a way of assessing how much fat cover a horse is carrying by looking at and feeling specific areas like the ribs, the crest of the neck, and around the tailhead, rather than just relying on weight alone, which can be misleading given differences in frame size. It usually uses a numbered scale, and the goal is to catch a horse trending toward overweight or underweight early, before it becomes a health problem. It matters a lot in practice because conditions like laminitis are strongly linked to excess weight, so regular scoring is one of the simplest preventative tools a yard has.

commonMistakes: Confusing body condition scoring with simply weighing the horse
Naming no specific areas of the body that are checked
Missing the link to preventing conditions like laminitis or malnutrition
followUps: What might make body condition scoring harder to do accurately on a very hairy native pony?

question: The equine industry covers everything from racing to therapy work. Which part interests you most, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine awareness of the breadth of the industry plus a reasoned, specific personal direction.

bullets: Show you know the industry has distinct sectors, not just 'working with horses'
Pick one direction and explain the specific reason it appeals
Stay open to how the course might shape or shift that interest
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I am most drawn to equine-assisted therapy work, partly from volunteering at a Riding for the Disabled centre where I saw how much confidence some children built just from grooming and leading a calm pony. That is different from performance or racing yards, where the horse's welfare and the client's goals can sometimes pull in different directions, and I like that therapy work tends to put the horse's temperament and wellbeing right at the centre. That said, I know this course covers a huge range of sectors and I want to stay open, since my current interest might shift once I have proper exposure to areas like stud work or equine science research.

commonMistakes: A vague answer like 'anything with horses' showing no industry awareness
Naming a sector with no personal reasoning behind it
Sounding completely closed off to anything else the course might offer
followUps: What skills do you think that sector particularly demands?

question: Tell us about a time you had to handle a horse that was frightened, in pain, or otherwise difficult. What did you do?
lookingFor: A real example showing calm judgement, safety awareness, and appropriate escalation when needed.

bullets: Describe a genuine, specific incident rather than a hypothetical
Show a calm, safety-first response rather than forcing the situation
Note when you sought help from someone more experienced, if relevant
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A young horse at the yard I work at spooked badly during a vet visit and pulled back hard against the lead rope, nearly getting loose in a busy area. I did not try to physically overpower him, instead I let the rope run through my hands rather than lock it, which stopped him hurting himself or me, and I moved to talk to him calmly once he had settled slightly rather than approaching straight away. Once he was steadier I called the yard manager over before continuing, because I knew a repeat spook in that state could genuinely be dangerous, and it taught me that staying calm myself is often more useful in the moment than any specific technique.

commonMistakes: Describing forcing or overpowering the horse as the solution
A hypothetical answer with no real personal experience
Failing to mention any safety awareness or escalation
followUps: What would you do differently if it happened again?

question: Why has biosecurity become such an important topic in the equine industry recently?
lookingFor: Awareness of real disease outbreaks and understanding of practical biosecurity measures.

bullets: Reference a real example, such as equine influenza or strangles outbreaks affecting yards or events
Explain why horses moving frequently between yards and events increases risk
Name at least one practical biosecurity measure, like isolation or vaccination
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Outbreaks like the equine influenza cases that led British Horseracing to cancel fixtures a few years ago really highlighted how fast disease can spread once horses start mixing at competitions and shared facilities. Because horses travel constantly between yards, shows, and studs, one infected animal can expose a huge number of others within days, which is very different from a closed herd situation. Practical measures like isolating new arrivals for a couple of weeks, keeping vaccination records current, and simple things like not sharing water buckets between yards at shows all make a real difference in slowing that spread.

commonMistakes: Giving no concrete real-world example
Discussing biosecurity in only vague terms like 'keeping things clean'
Not connecting the risk to how the industry actually moves horses around
followUps: What would you do differently as a yard manager if a horse arrived from a competition showing a cough?

question: How would feeding differ between a horse in light hacking work and one competing at a high level of eventing?
lookingFor: Understanding that energy and nutrient needs scale with workload, with forage still as the base.

bullets: State that forage should remain the foundation for both horses
Explain that harder-working horses need more energy, usually from concentrates or fat sources
Mention increased need for things like electrolytes or protein quality at higher workloads
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Both horses should have forage as the base of their diet, but the light hacking horse might need very little else beyond good hay and a balancer to cover vitamins and minerals. The eventer, especially one doing fast work and cross-country, needs considerably more energy than forage alone can safely provide, so that usually comes from concentrates or oil-based supplements, along with attention to electrolyte replacement after sweating heavily. The eventer also needs good quality protein to support muscle recovery, so the whole diet has to be built around a much higher and more carefully balanced energy demand, not just more food of the same kind.

commonMistakes: Suggesting simply feeding more of everything without considering forage as base
Ignoring electrolyte or hydration needs for harder-working horses
Treating all concentrate feeds as interchangeable regardless of workload
followUps: Why can overfeeding concentrates to a lightly worked horse be a problem?

question: What are the most critical things to get right in the first few days of a foal's life?
lookingFor: Awareness of colostrum, early bonding, and basic monitoring for a newborn foal.

bullets: Mention colostrum intake within the first hours as critical for passive immunity
Note the importance of the foal standing and nursing within a reasonable window
Reference basic monitoring, like checking the mare's milk and the foal passing meconium
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Getting colostrum into the foal within the first few hours is probably the single most critical thing, because that first milk carries antibodies the foal cannot get any other way, and the gut's ability to absorb them drops off sharply after about twelve hours. Alongside that, you want to see the foal standing and nursing on its own reasonably quickly, usually within a couple of hours, since a foal that is slow to do that can signal an underlying problem. Monitoring things like whether the foal passes its first stool, the meconium, without straining also matters, because impaction there is a common early issue that needs quick attention.

commonMistakes: Not mentioning colostrum or passive immunity at all
Vague statements like 'keep the foal warm' with no physiological reasoning
Confusing foal care priorities with general adult horse care
followUps: Why does the timing of colostrum intake matter so much?

question: 'Wastage' in racing and breeding, where horses bred for performance do not make the grade, is a controversial topic. What is your view on it?
lookingFor: Balanced, well-informed reasoning that acknowledges complexity rather than a slogan-level answer.

bullets: Show understanding of what wastage actually refers to, in breeding and racing
Present more than one perspective, such as industry economics versus welfare concerns
Reach a considered personal position rather than refusing to engage
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Wastage refers to the fact that a large proportion of horses bred for racing or top-level sport never end up competing at that level, and what happens to those horses afterwards is genuinely contested. Some in the industry argue that breeding numbers reflect a competitive selection process similar to other sports, and that good aftercare charities now rehome many horses successfully into second careers. My own view is that the industry has made real progress with traceability and retraining schemes, but I think there is still a responsibility gap around horses bred by smaller or less scrupulous breeders who are not connected to those support networks, and that is where I would want to see more regulation.

commonMistakes: A one-sided rant with no acknowledgement of the other side
Not actually defining what wastage means
Refusing to give any personal opinion at all
followUps: What kind of policy change do you think would actually help?

question: Can you give an example of a horse breed and explain how its physical traits suit the work it is traditionally used for?
lookingFor: Ability to connect breed conformation or traits to functional purpose, showing real subject knowledge.

bullets: Name a specific breed accurately
Describe a real physical or temperament trait of that breed
Explain clearly how that trait suits its traditional use
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The Shire horse is a good example, it was bred as a heavy draught horse, so it has a large frame, substantial bone, and powerful hindquarters built for pulling heavy loads at a steady pace rather than speed. That conformation, along with a generally calm temperament, made it ideal for farm work and hauling before mechanisation took over those jobs. Compare that with something like a Thoroughbred, which has a lighter frame and longer stride built for speed over distance, and you can see how differently breeds have been shaped by the specific job they were developed for.

commonMistakes: Naming a breed with no real understanding of its traits
Describing traits with no connection to functional purpose
Factually incorrect claims about a breed's characteristics
followUps: Can you think of a breed developed for a completely different purpose?

question: How has best practice around worming horses changed in recent years, and why?
lookingFor: Awareness of the shift from blanket dosing to targeted, evidence-based parasite control.

bullets: Note the historic approach of routine, calendar-based worming for all horses
Explain the shift toward testing, like faecal egg counts, to target treatment
Give the reason for the change, mainly anthelmintic resistance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It used to be standard to worm every horse on a yard on a fixed rotational schedule regardless of whether they actually needed it, but that approach has been largely replaced because it was accelerating resistance to the drugs themselves. The current best practice is to use faecal egg counts to test individual horses periodically and only treat the ones actually showing a significant worm burden, alongside good pasture management like poo picking. The main driver of that change is that resistant parasite populations are a genuine and growing problem, so using wormers more selectively is about preserving their effectiveness for when they are truly needed.

commonMistakes: Describing only the old blanket approach with no awareness of the shift
Not mentioning resistance as the underlying reason for the change
Confusing faecal egg counts with a general health checkup
followUps: What non-chemical pasture management steps help reduce worm burden?

question: What do you think you would bring to this course and to your fellow students, beyond your grades?
lookingFor: Genuine self-awareness about a specific strength or experience that adds value to a cohort.

bullets: Name a specific skill or experience, not a generic trait like 'hard work'
Give evidence that it is real, not just claimed
Connect it to how it might help other students or the course community
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think I would bring a genuinely practical, yard-honed instinct for horse handling that comes from three years of daily hands-on work, which some students coming more from a classroom background might not have built up yet. I have already found myself helping newer volunteers at my yard get comfortable around nervous horses, and I enjoy that side of things as much as the science itself. I think that combination, being willing to share practical know-how while still being genuinely curious about the underlying theory, is something I would bring into group project work especially.

commonMistakes: A generic claim like 'I work hard' with no specific evidence
Talking only about personal achievement with no mention of others
Overstating expertise they do not actually have
followUps: Can you think of a specific moment you have already helped someone else learn something horse-related?

question: What environmental challenges do you think the equine industry faces, and how might the science help address them?
lookingFor: Awareness that horse-keeping has real environmental impacts and some grasp of science-based responses.

bullets: Name a real environmental issue, such as land use, manure management, or water use
Explain briefly why it is a genuine challenge for the industry
Suggest a science-informed response, such as improved grazing management or manure composting
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Manure management is a bigger environmental issue than people often realise, a single horse can produce a huge volume of waste a year, and poorly managed it can contribute to nutrient runoff into local waterways. Overgrazing is another real problem, since horses graze differently to cattle and can badly degrade pasture if stocking density is not carefully managed. I think the science side genuinely helps here, things like rotational grazing systems based on pasture growth data, and composting manure properly instead of just stockpiling it, are both evidence-based practices that reduce the environmental footprint without compromising horse welfare.

commonMistakes: Vague environmental concern with no specific equine-industry example
Ignoring the science-based solution half of the question
Conflating equine sustainability issues with general farming issues with no equine specificity
followUps: How might climate change specifically affect pasture management for horse owners?

question: Equine science sometimes involves advice changing as new research comes out, like around feeding or training methods. How would you approach a situation where new evidence contradicts something you were taught?
lookingFor: Intellectual flexibility and a genuinely scientific attitude toward evidence, rather than defensiveness.

bullets: Show willingness to update views based on quality evidence rather than clinging to prior belief
Mention evaluating the strength or source of the new evidence critically, not accepting it blindly either
Give a real or plausible example of practice changing due to research
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would want to actually look at the evidence itself before deciding what to do with it, checking things like sample size and whether it has been replicated, rather than either dismissing it because it contradicts what I was taught or accepting it uncritically just because it is new. A good example is how thinking around stabling has shifted, older advice often prioritised keeping horses stalled and protected, while more recent behavioural research strongly supports maximising turnout and social contact for welfare. I think being a good scientist in this field means being willing to say I was taught something that current evidence no longer fully supports, and updating my practice accordingly rather than being precious about it.

commonMistakes: Refusing to consider that established practice could be wrong
Accepting any new claim uncritically with no evaluation of evidence quality
Giving an entirely abstract answer with no concrete equine example
followUps: Can you think of a piece of traditional horse-keeping advice you now think is outdated?
